title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem and CRT Lattice Connections
description: Dirichlet's approximation theorem (1842): for any real α and N ≥ 1, there exist p, q with 1 ≤ q ≤ N and |qα - p| < 1/N. Proved via pigeonhole principle on fractional part binning. Includes mediant/Stern-Brocot property, lattice point theorem, golden ratio identities, and CRT non-coprime solvability examples connecting Diophantine approximation to lattice geometry.

overview.historicalContext:
Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet (1805-1859) proved this theorem in 1842, establishing the foundation of Diophantine approximation. The result shows that every real number can be well-approximated by rationals, with quality inversely proportional to the denominator. The proof introduced the 'pigeonhole principle' (Schubfachprinzip) to number theory.

The theorem was later refined by Hurwitz (1891), who showed the optimal constant is 1/√5, achieved by the golden ratio φ = (1+√5)/2. The connection to the Chinese Remainder Theorem arises through lattice geometry: CRT solvability corresponds to lattice coset membership, and Dirichlet-style counting arguments on lattice points yield approximation results.

The Stern-Brocot tree (Stern 1858, Brocot 1861) provides the algorithmic structure for generating best rational approximations, with the mediant operation as its fundamental building block. This connects to continued fractions, which give the sequence of best approximations to any real number.
overview.problemStatement:
**Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem**: For any real number α and any positive integer N, there exist integers p and q with 1 ≤ q ≤ N such that |qα - p| < 1/N.

Equivalently: |α - p/q| < 1/(qN) ≤ 1/q².

This is proved via the pigeonhole principle: N+1 fractional parts {0·α}, {1·α}, ..., {N·α} mapped to N bins of width 1/N in [0,1). Two must share a bin, giving a good approximation.
overview.text: Dirichlet's approximation theorem via pigeonhole principle, with connections to CRT lattice theory, Stern-Brocot mediants, and the golden ratio as the worst-case approximation target.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Dirichlet's theorem** is proved by defining a bin function binFn : Fin(N+1) → Fin(N) that maps each index i to the bin ⌊N · fract(iα)⌋. By Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt (pigeonhole), two indices share a bin. Their fractional parts are within 1/N, and the difference gives the desired approximation.

The **mediant theorem** uses cross-multiplication: a/b < c/d implies a·d < c·b, and the mediant (a+c)/(b+d) satisfies both a(b+d) < (a+c)b and (a+c)d < c(b+d).

The **golden ratio** identities follow from √5² = 5 and algebraic manipulation with nlinarith.
keyInsights: **Pigeonhole on fractional parts**: The N+1 values {kα} for k = 0,...,N lie in [0,1). Binning into N intervals of width 1/N guarantees a collision, which yields the approximation. The proof is entirely constructive once the collision is found.

**Cast gymnastics**: The main technical challenge is managing coercions between ℕ, ℤ, and ℝ. Natural subtraction (j - i where j > i as ℕ) must be cast to real subtraction (↑j - ↑i) via Nat.cast_sub, and integer floor differences must be split via Int.cast_sub.

**Golden ratio optimality**: φ = (1+√5)/2 is the hardest-to-approximate irrational because its continued fraction [1;1,1,...] has the slowest convergence. Hurwitz's theorem says 1/√5 is the best universal constant for |x - p/q| < C/q².

**CRT-lattice duality**: Non-coprime CRT solvability (gcd(m₁,m₂) | (a₁-a₂)) is equivalent to a lattice point existing in a shifted sublattice. This geometric viewpoint unifies Dirichlet-style counting with modular arithmetic.

**Stern-Brocot mediant**: The mediant (a+c)/(b+d) of a/b and c/d always lies strictly between them. This operation generates all rationals in lowest terms and produces best approximations via binary search.

sections.title: Pigeonhole Setup for Fractional Part Binning
sections.summary: Defines the bin function binFn : Fin(N+1) → Fin(N) mapping index i to ⌊N · fract(iα)⌋, with supporting lemmas for well-typedness (floor non-negative, floor < N) and the key same_bin_fract_close lemma showing colliding bins imply fractional parts within 1/N.
sections.mathContext: Pigeonhole setup for Dirichlet's theorem: define `binFn : Fin(N+1) → Fin(N)` mapping $i \mapsto \lfloor N \cdot \{i\alpha\} \rfloor$, where $\{\cdot\}$ denotes the fractional part. Since $N+1 > N$, the pigeonhole principle guarantees two indices with the same bin.

sections.title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem
sections.summary: Proves Dirichlet's approximation theorem: for any real α and N ≥ 1, there exist p, q with 1 ≤ q ≤ N and |qα - p| < 1/N. Applies pigeonhole via Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt to binFn, then converts the bin collision to an approximation bound through fract_sub_eq and careful cast gymnastics.
sections.mathContext: Dirichlet's approximation theorem: for any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and $N \geq 1$, there exist $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $1 \leq q \leq N$ and $|q\alpha - p| < 1/N$. Equivalently, $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/(qN) \leq 1/q^2$.

sections.title: Consequences: Nearest Integer Bound
sections.summary: Derives the nearest integer bound: every real number has an integer within distance 1/2. A direct corollary using the floor of α + 1/2.
sections.mathContext: Consequences: every real number has a nearest integer within distance $1/2$. Also: for irrational $\alpha$, there are infinitely many rationals $p/q$ with $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/q^2$ (by letting $N \to \infty$).

sections.title: Lattice Point Theorem
sections.summary: Proves integer_in_interval (any interval [a, a+1) contains an integer via ceiling) and lattice_point_exists (any interval (a, a+m] contains a multiple of m), providing the geometric foundation for CRT solvability through lattice coset arguments.
sections.mathContext: Integer-in-interval: every half-open interval $[a, a+1)$ contains an integer ($\lceil a \rceil$). Lattice point existence: intervals of length $\geq 1$ in $\mathbb{R}$ contain at least one integer.

sections.title: Mediant and Stern-Brocot Property
sections.summary: Proves the mediant (a+c)/(b+d) lies strictly between a/b and c/d via cross-multiplication, and that Farey neighbors (determinant cb - ad = 1) are automatically ordered. These results underlie the Stern-Brocot tree construction of best rational approximations.
sections.mathContext: The mediant property: if $a/b < c/d$ (with $b, d > 0$), then $a/b < (a+c)/(b+d) < c/d$. Proved by cross-multiplication: $a(b+d) < b(a+c)$ iff $ad < bc$. This is the basis of the Stern-Brocot tree.

sections.title: Golden Ratio Properties
sections.summary: Defines φ = (1+√5)/2 and proves its key algebraic identities: positivity, φ > 1, φ² = φ + 1, 1/φ = φ - 1, and the minimal polynomial root property. Includes Fibonacci verification examples showing the denominators of φ's best rational approximations.
sections.mathContext: The golden ratio $\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2$: key identities $\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$, $\varphi > 1$, and $\varphi$ is the 'hardest to approximate' irrational — its continued fraction $[1;1,1,1,\ldots]$ has the slowest convergence among all irrationals (Hurwitz's theorem).

sections.title: CRT Non-Coprime Lattice Examples
sections.summary: Concrete computational examples: a solvable non-coprime system (x ≡ 3 mod 6, x ≡ 1 mod 4 → x = 9 mod 12), an unsolvable system (gcd doesn't divide residue difference), Bézout witness verification, and the classical Sunzi problem for coprime moduli.
sections.mathContext: Concrete CRT examples: the non-coprime system $x \equiv 3 \pmod{6}$, $x \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ has solution $x = 9$ (checking: $9 = 6+3$ and $9 = 2 \cdot 4 + 1$). Demonstrates that CRT extends beyond coprime moduli when compatibility conditions hold.

crossReferences.description: Extends the non-coprime CRT formalization with Dirichlet's approximation theorem, connecting lattice geometry to Diophantine approximation
The constructive CRT computes solutions for coprime moduli; this file extends to non-coprime solvability and Diophantine approximation
The pigeonhole principle used in Dirichlet's theorem is the same combinatorial tool that yields Euclid's proof of infinite primes via counting arguments
Bézout's identity provides the coefficient witness for CRT solvability: the examples use 6·(-1) + 4·2 = gcd(6,4) to construct solutions

conclusion.summary: We have formalized Dirichlet's approximation theorem via the pigeonhole principle, establishing the foundational result of Diophantine approximation. The proof demonstrates how finite combinatorics (pigeonhole on N+1 fractional parts) yields a powerful analytic result (rational approximation quality 1/(qN)). The connections to CRT lattice structure, Stern-Brocot mediants, and the golden ratio show how number theory, combinatorics, and geometry interweave in the theory of Diophantine approximation.
conclusion.implications:
**1. Diophantine approximation**: Every irrational $\alpha$ has infinitely many rational approximations $p/q$ satisfying $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/q^2$. Hurwitz's theorem (1891) sharpens this to $1/(\sqrt{5}q^2)$ — optimal because the golden ratio $\phi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2$ is the worst-approximable irrational.

**2. Lattice connections**: CRT solvability for non-coprime moduli reduces to lattice point counting — the system $x \equiv a_i \pmod{m_i}$ is solvable iff $\gcd(m_i, m_j) \mid (a_i - a_j)$ for all pairs, connecting number theory to the geometry of numbers.

**3. Higher-dimensional extensions**: Dirichlet's method extends via Minkowski's theorem to simultaneous approximation: for $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \mathbb{R}$, there exist integers with $|\alpha_i - p_i/q| < 1/q^{1+1/n}$ for all $i$.

**4. Transcendence theory**: Roth's theorem (1955, Fields Medal) proves $|\alpha - p/q| > c_\varepsilon/q^{2+\varepsilon}$ for algebraic $\alpha$ — matching Dirichlet's bound up to $\varepsilon$ and providing the sharpest known measure of irrationality for algebraic numbers.
openQuestions: Can the pigeonhole-based proof be extended to simultaneous Diophantine approximation in Lean, formalizing Minkowski's lattice point theorem for convex bodies?
What is the formal relationship between the Stern-Brocot mediant operation and the convergents of continued fraction expansions — can this be unified in Lean's Mathlib?
The Littlewood conjecture (1930, still open): for all real α, β, is it true that lim inf n·‖nα‖·‖nβ‖ = 0? This is the natural two-dimensional extension of Dirichlet's theorem.
